analysis.title: Weekly Macro and Markets View, Week 47 2026
key_insights: US October CPI rose 0.4% on the month against 0.3% expected, and core rose 0.3% against 0.2% expected. This is the third upside surprise in three CPI prints. Energy prices contributed, but core services and goods inflation are also picking up slightly.
US Treasury yields rose sharply. The 10yr yield moved back above 5% and the weekly rise in 2yr yields was the largest in over 2 years. Yields remain below their early October peak.

Fed Governor Christopher Waller discussed a possible hike in December at double the standard size (the extracted text shows '50' with the unit missing, so this is read as a 50bp hike against the standard 25bp). Markets price three further hikes between December and next June, one more than at the start of November.
New Fed Chair Kevin Warsh prefers less communication, which makes market reactions to incoming data more volatile. Other voting members still publish their own views.
The US dollar strengthened with yields. The DXY index reached its highest level since April 2025.

Equities rebounded across most sectors after a sharp post-US-election sell-off that Zurich judges to have been technically driven. US and Korean semiconductors gave back some gains on Friday amid Nvidia-related uncertainty.

Credit held up without having sold off the prior week. Spreads tightened across ratings in the US and Europe, led by high yield, with US HY fund inflows and oversubscribed US IG deals taking monthly IG volume to USD 117bn. US HY issuance nearly stopped late in the week when Treasuries sold off after the CPI print.
Zurich's positioning view is that stock prospects look constructive with solid fundamentals, while corporate credit offers limited upside because spreads are historically tight.

UK Q3 GDP grew 0.7% QoQ, with private consumption +0.6% and business investment +1.7% QoQ. Net exports were a small drag, which Zurich attributes to imports reflecting technology investment. Inflation is rising, the Bank of England has a more restrictive stance, and Zurich expects high rates and energy costs to weigh somewhat on 2027 growth.
The KPMG/REC Jobs Report showed slower permanent hiring in October and modestly higher redundancies in the UK.

China's October data weakened. Retail sales rose 0.4% YoY with auto sales down 21.4%, and fixed-asset investment fell 8.1% YTD across infrastructure, manufacturing and property. Exports rose 35.2% YoY in USD terms, driven by tech, as weak domestic demand and excess capacity push manufacturers overseas.

Zurich sees a widening two-speed Chinese economy, with export-led high-tech manufacturing strong and consumption and non-tech investment weak. It argues this supports bolder fiscal stimulus in 2027, particularly a faster rollout of the 'Six Networks' infrastructure programme (communication networks, data centres, power grids, renewables, logistics).

Brazil's fiscal package targets BRL 50-60bn (about 0.5% of GDP) in 2027 savings, below the BRL 70-80bn in earlier press reports. It relies mostly on revenue measures with conditional spending restraint, local rates reacted little, and Zurich expects further measures to be needed.

Brazil's October CPI was 0.1% MoM, a downside surprise with easing underlying services inflation. Annual inflation rose to 4.6% YoY, above the 4.5% upper limit. BCB minutes fit Zurich's expectation of an extended pause.

The US Senate voted 73-25 on November 9 to open debate on the bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, clearing the first 60-vote hurdle. Zurich expects it to pass. It would streamline NEPA permitting reviews, amend the Federal Power Act to ease grid connection bottlenecks, and under the Ratepayer Protection Act require large data centre developers to cover their own energy infrastructure costs. Zurich calls it a positive for clean energy.

sector_views.rationale: Faster permitting and grid connections under the Senate bill would address bottlenecks in renewable integration, which Zurich sees as a positive development for the sector.
Fundamentals are solid and demand is strong, but spreads are historically tight, so Zurich sees limited upside.
Zurich calls the post-election sell-off technically driven and says prospects for stocks look constructive with fundamentals still solid.

macro_indicators.interpretation: Third consecutive upside CPI surprise. It pushed Treasury yields higher and raised pricing of Fed hikes.
Underlying inflation in core services and goods is picking up slightly, beyond the energy effect.
Back above 5% but still below the early October peak. The rise halted US HY issuance late in the week.

Solid growth supported by consumption and business investment. Zurich expects some drag from high rates and energy costs into 2027.
Weak consumption, with auto sales down 21.4%. Supports the case for more fiscal stimulus.
Infrastructure, manufacturing and property investment all contracted, while high-tech investment held up.
Driven by tech exports as weak domestic demand pushes output overseas.
Downside surprise with easing underlying services inflation.
Above the 4.5% upper limit of the target range. Zurich expects an extended BCB pause.

risk_factors: Further upside US inflation surprises could lead to a 50bp-sized December hike and a higher yield path.
Warsh's preference for less Fed communication raises the volatility of market responses to data.
Historically tight credit spreads leave limited upside, and a Treasury sell-off can halt HY issuance.
Nvidia-related uncertainty is weighing on US and Korean semiconductors.
Rising energy prices and inflation in the UK, combined with high rates, are likely to weigh on growth into 2027.
Brazil's fiscal adjustment relies on revenue measures with conditional spending restraint, so the debt trajectory may need further measures.
China's weak consumption and contracting non-tech investment cycle point to a need for more fiscal support.
vol_and_positioning: Zurich judges the post-US-election equity sell-off to have been technically driven. Risk assets recovered across most sectors, though US and Korean semiconductors reversed some gains on Friday on Nvidia-related uncertainty.
US HY issuance nearly stopped late in the week when the 10yr yield rose above 5%. US HY funds still received inflows and US IG deals were oversubscribed.
